title: Shannon Entropy
body:
$$
\begin{align*}
H(x) &= \mathbf{E}[I(x)] \\
&=-\mathbf{E}(\log(P(x))) \\
&= -\sum_{x=0}^1P(x)\log(P(x))
\end{align*}

$$

$\mathbf{E}[\cdot]$ here is expectation over a [[Probability Distribution]]; see
[[Random Variable]] in [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234) for what that operator means and why
$E[g(X)] \neq g(E[X])$.

---

**Expected surprise.** [[Information]] measures how startling one outcome is; entropy averages that
over every outcome, weighted by how often it happens, giving a single number for the whole
distribution. Evan's third line above writes the two-outcome case, summing $x$ over $\{0,1\}$; in
general the sum runs over every outcome the [[Random Variable]] can take.

Two readings, both worth holding:

- **Uncertainty.** How much you do not know about the next draw, in bits.
- **Code length.** The average number of bits per symbol of the best possible code for this source.
  Shannon's source coding theorem says you cannot beat $H$, and can get arbitrarily close.

## The shape of it

For a coin with $P(\text{heads}) = p$:

| $p$ | $H$ | |
|---|---|---|
| $0$ | $0$ bits | certain, nothing to learn |
| $0.1$ | $0.47$ bits | mostly predictable |
| $0.5$ | $\mathbf{1}$ bit | maximally uncertain |
| $0.9$ | $0.47$ bits | mostly predictable, the other way |
| $1$ | $0$ bits | certain again |

**Entropy is maximised by the uniform distribution and zero only when the outcome is certain.** For
$n$ equally likely outcomes $H = \log_2 n$, which recovers the plain counting fact that $n$
possibilities need $\log_2 n$ bits. Everything you know about the source is a departure from
uniform, and every departure lowers $H$, which is why compression works at all: the entropy is the
floor, and the gap between $\log_2 n$ and $H$ is what a compressor gets to keep.

The convention $0\log 0 = 0$ is standard and follows from the limit, so impossible outcomes
contribute nothing.

## Its relationship to the other three

$H(P)$ is the **best case**, the cost of coding $P$ when you know $P$. [[Cross-Entropy]] $H(P,Q)$
is what you actually pay using a model $Q$, and it is never smaller. [[KL Divergence]] is the
difference. Written once:

$$
H(P,Q) = H(P) + D_{KL}(P \,\|\, Q)
$$

That identity is the reason [[Cross-Entropy Loss]] is the loss: $H(P)$ is a property of the data,
so training cannot change it, and minimising the left side is minimising the divergence on the
right.

## Not the thermodynamic one

Same formula up to a constant, and Shannon took the name on von Neumann's advice, but this note is
about messages. [[Entropy]] carries the disambiguation.

## Related

- [[Information]]: the per-outcome quantity being averaged
- [[Cross-Entropy]], [[KL Divergence]], [[Cross-Entropy Loss]]
- [[Information Theory]], [[Entropy]]
- [[Variance]] ([[STATISTICS]], MATH 2234): the other "how spread out is this" number, and not the
  same one; entropy does not care what the outcome *values* are, only their probabilities
